sources.title: Lands FAQ
sources.annotation: Read the complete substantive FAQ. Separates corporate holdings, traditional-use lands, Chitina Native Corporation property, access permits and reserved easements; also addresses research and commercial filming. This is the landholder’s published account, not a title search or complete legal determination of a particular route. Undated acreage and pending selections are not independently verified as current. Link-specific permits and maps were not audited.

sources.title: History — Chitina
sources.annotation: Read the entire page: corporate history, relationship to Native Village of Chitina and six named historical biographies. Distinguishes shareholders from the separate local tribe. Leadership, family and place-name accounts are attributed corporate public history; approximate dates retain their uncertainty. The 2004 population estimate is historical, not current, and no ceremonial explanation is reproduced.

sources.title: Land — Chitina
sources.annotation: Read the complete land and permitting statement. Explains surface-estate ownership, stewardship for future generations, shareholder/descendant priorities, public access and permission. Distinct from the historical biographies. Treat ownership acreage as the corporation’s undated self-report and access language as its stated policy; neither establishes boundaries, title to every parcel or all legal exceptions. No permit purchased or request submitted.

sources.title: Gulkana Community Master Plan — Public Review Draft, January 25, 2024
sources.publisher: Gulkana Village Council; prepared by Agnew::Beck Consulting
sources.annotation: Read cover and printed pp.3–6,9–12,21–22,25–28; visually checked pp.5–6 and28. Council-led planning includes residents’ survey responses and proposed housing, cultural, safety and environmental work. The 23-response survey also invited non-Tribal members. This is explicitly a public review draft, not verified adopted policy or evidence that proposed projects were completed. Maps and exact cultural-site locations are not reproduced.
sources.author: Agnew::Beck Consulting, for Gulkana Village Council

sources.title: Village Highlight — Tazlina, Kanas, Fall 2018, p.8
sources.annotation: Read the complete printed/PDF page8 article and visually checked the original layout. Reports Tazlina’s contamination-response work, recycling and a completed heating project, while describing a walkway as still planned. This dated Indigenous corporate publication discusses the Village’s programs; no individual author is identified. Do not turn its 2018 ownership context, project status or cleanup account into a present legal or environmental finding.

supportingSources.title: About the Ahtna Intertribal Resource Commission
supportingSources.annotation: Read the complete substantive About text, membership, territory description and simplified timeline. Supports the 2011 coordinating role, eight member tribes and two corporate landholders. Short institutional overview retained outside this batch’s substantive minimum. Its timeline’s broad statements about state authority and federal subsistence law are not adopted as legal analysis; territory graphics are not title boundaries.

supportingSources.title: Ahtna Villages
supportingSources.annotation: Read the complete short prose statement naming eight regional villages and describing the 1980 merger of seven village corporations, with Chitina remaining separate. The statement concerns corporations, not dissolution or merger of village tribal governments. Short supporting institutional reference only; the interactive map was not audited for boundaries or access rights.

supportingSources.title: Ahtna History & Culture
supportingSources.annotation: Read the complete substantive prose and captions surrounding resource links. Describes the Copper River name, seasonal family food work and continuing practices; shareholder totals are not a people’s census. Short overview/resource gateway kept outside the substantive minimum. Linked videos, books, lesson pages and Smithsonian items are not represented as read or watched. Undated language/dialect claims require specialist context.

supportingSources.title: About Us — Native Village of Gakona
supportingSources.annotation: Read the complete short page describing sovereign government, services, council and justices. Useful village-published corroboration that a tribal institution supplies social, environmental and justice services, distinct from corporate landholding. Short service/staff directory kept outside the substantive count; no current staffing or service availability inferred beyond the posted account.

proposedParagraphs.title: Landholding and traditional-use geography
proposedParagraphs.text: Ahtna, Incorporated’s land FAQ distinguishes the property it owns from a much larger traditional-use landscape. It also identifies Chitina Native Corporation as a separate landholder. The FAQ describes different arrangements for recreation, research, filming and reserved public routes. These distinctions matter when reading a map: cultural relationships, corporate ownership and particular access rights describe different things. The corporation’s general account does not determine every parcel or route’s legal status.

proposedParagraphs.title: Chitina’s own public history
proposedParagraphs.text: Chitina Native Corporation dates its incorporation to 1973 and describes shareholders as primarily residents or descendants of the Native Village of Chitina, which it identifies as a separate tribe. Its public history recalls named leaders including Nicolai, Hanagita and Goodlataw, and Doc Billum’s river transport and knowledge of copper deposits. These attributed biographies place particular people and family relationships within exploration, transport and mining histories; their approximate dates should remain qualified.

proposedParagraphs.title: Stewardship and corporate responsibilities
proposedParagraphs.text: Chitina’s distinct land statement connects cultural history and food resources with responsibilities to future generations. It gives shareholders and descendants priority in cultural, subsistence and recreational use while describing conditions for public access. This is the corporation’s account of managing its property. It should be read alongside current permissions and the status of particular land, rather than treating a broad Ahtna regional label as either public access or one uniform ownership.

proposedParagraphs.title: A Gulkana planning conversation
proposedParagraphs.text: Gulkana’s January 2024 public review draft master plan connects cultural life with housing, training, community facilities and environmental resilience. A small 2023 survey, open to Tribal and non-Tribal respondents, records local concerns and aspirations; it is not a census of Ahtna opinion. Proposed actions include protecting cultural places, improving housing and providing additional subsistence-skills learning. The draft shows a particular community considering its future, without establishing final adoption or completed construction.

proposedParagraphs.title: Tazlina’s practical environmental work
proposedParagraphs.text: A Fall 2018 Kanas article describes Tazlina’s effort to address contamination around the former Copper Valley School, including work on land the Village did not then own. It connects environmental programs with community access, recycling and energy needs, reporting a heating project completed that September. A pedestrian route remained in planning. The account shows village initiative across institutional and property constraints at that date; it is not a current ownership record or contamination clearance.

optionalSupportingParagraphs.title: Connected institutions with distinct roles
optionalSupportingParagraphs.text: AITRC identifies eight member tribes and the landholding corporations Ahtna, Incorporated and Chitina Native Corporation. It describes coordinating resource work rather than replacing village governments. Ahtna’s short village history also explains that seven village corporations merged with the regional corporation in 1980 while Chitina’s remained separate. That corporate reorganization should not be confused with a merger of tribal governments. Gakona’s own page separately describes its government and community services.

optionalSupportingParagraphs.title: Seasonal work in the corporate cultural account
optionalSupportingParagraphs.text: Ahtna’s cultural overview places family food work within a seasonal rhythm and emphasizes continuing subsistence practices. Its shareholder information describes a corporate constituency, rather than counting everyone who belongs to the people or language community.

countRecommendation.note: Ahtna Lands FAQ enriches the existing lands record, not a duplicate new work. Existing AITRC About and History & Culture are refreshed supporting references. Chitina historical biographies and its separately published land statement have distinct subjects. The Kanas count is one inspected article, not every item in the issue.

geographicFindings.name: Native Village of Gakona
geographicFindings.description: Village-published home page places Gakona at the confluence of the Copper and Gakona Rivers in Alaska’s Ahtna region.
geographicFindings.precision: Named river confluence, broad community location only; no geocoding
geographicFindings.qualification: Supporting home-page geography, not a boundary, title determination, public access claim or sensitive-site location.

rightsFindings.subject: Landowner statements and access rights
rightsFindings.finding: Separate Native corporate landholders publish their own permissions and permitting information. Ahtna FAQ explicitly distinguishes traditional-use geography, owned lands and reserved public easements.
rightsFindings.precision: General published landholder statements; not legal advice or adjudication of any specific easement, road, parcel or waterway.

researchGaps: The Gulkana PDF is a January 25, 2024 public review draft. No final adopted plan or adoption resolution was located in the bounded website/domain search.

The survey has 23 responses and invited non-Tribal respondents. Its priority chart says choose up to three yet the displayed item counts total 100, exceeding 23×3; do not calculate shares or statistically representative rankings without the underlying instrument/data.
Corporate acreage, pending land selections and public access conditions were read as undated self-descriptions, not verified parcel-by-parcel legal facts.
The 2018 Tazlina article is not evidence of current ownership, program staffing, complete environmental remediation or completed planned walkway; later village sources should extend this account.

Village-authored accounts for Cantwell, Mentasta, Cheesh’na, Kluti-Kaah and Chitina tribal government remain desirable. The eight AITRC members do not define the complete range of every person’s cultural affiliation.
No current population, shareholder or speaker count is used as a census of the entire Ahtna people.
integrationNotes: Distinguish people/language, village tribal governments, ANCSA corporations and the intertribal coordinating body. The 1980 merger concerned village corporations, not tribal governments.
All five substantive sources are used in proposedParagraphs. Supporting institutional cards remain outside the minimum, even where used in optional prose.

Each candidate’s draftDerivedWordCount conservatively counts its entire annotation plus every cited paragraph, and remains under 200 words. Remove the scratch count field on integration if unnecessary.
No Foundation reconstruction domain used; linked cultural or language works not independently opened are leads only.
No maps, exact archaeological/cemetery/cultural-place coordinates, private contact details or images are proposed for reproduction. Cached originals stay outside served assets.

Root reserves technical fisheries/co-stewardship, federal agreements and court sources; the language/specialist agents handle Foundation/language and longer historical studies. This draft does not duplicate those reviews.
